channel.description: Recent content in coast on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Amanoseki Fishing Village — Guide
item.description: Along the coast near Usa in northern Oita, small fishing villages like Amanoseki offer a quiet, authentic glimpse of everyday coastal life away from the tourist trail. Here fishing boats bob in a working harbour, nets dry in the sun, and the daily rhythm of the sea still shapes the community much as it has for generations. Visitors can enjoy the relaxed seaside atmosphere, the scenery of the bay and its boats, and — above all — exceptionally fresh local seafood straight from the catch, served simply at local eateries or bought at the harbour.

item.title: Beppu's Hot-Spring Beaches — Guide
item.description: Beppu’s setting on a bay backed by volcanic mountains means its abundant hot springs reach right down to the coast, creating rare seaside bathing experiences. Along the shore, hot-spring facilities and beaches let visitors enjoy the geothermal waters with open views over Beppu Bay and the Kunisaki Peninsula beyond — soaking in seaside open-air baths, being buried in naturally heated sand on the beach, or bathing as the sun rises or sets over the water.

item.title: Cape Manzamo — Guide
item.description: Cape Manzamo (Manzamo), on the west coast of Okinawa’s main island in Onna Village, is one of the island’s most iconic and photographed scenic spots. Its defining feature is a striking cliff of raised coral limestone whose profile resembles an elephant’s trunk or head dipping into the sea, framed by clear turquoise water below and open ocean beyond. The name Manzamo means ‘a field for ten thousand people to sit’, a phrase attributed to an 18th-century Ryukyuan king who admired the sweeping grassy clifftop.

item.title: Cape Sata: Japan's Southern Tip — Guide
item.description: Cape Sata (Sata-misaki), at the tip of the Osumi Peninsula, is the southernmost point of mainland Japan (Kyushu), a wild and scenic headland marking the very edge of the country’s main islands. Reached by a scenic drive down the peninsula and a walk through lush subtropical vegetation, the cape offers dramatic coastal scenery: rugged cliffs plunging into the deep blue sea, sweeping views across the water, and on clear days sightings of distant islands including Yakushima and Tanegashima on the horizon.

item.title: Cape Soya (Northernmost Point) — Guide
item.description: Cape Soya (Soya Misaki), near Wakkanai at the far northern tip of Hokkaido, marks the northernmost point of mainland Japan — a milestone destination for travellers who want to reach the very top of the country. The cape’s iconic landmark is the triangular Monument of the Northernmost Point of Japan, a popular photo spot pointing symbolically toward the North Star. Standing on this windswept, grassy headland looking out over the Soya Strait, on clear days you can even make out the faint outline of Sakhalin (Russian territory) about 43 km across the water.

item.title: Genkai Seaside Park — Guide
item.description: Genkai Seaside Park, on the scenic northern coast of Saga facing the Genkai Sea, is a spacious coastal park that makes a relaxed family destination. Its wide lawns, gardens and open spaces are planted with seasonal flowers that add colour through the year, and paths lead to viewpoints and walks along the shore with views over the sea and coastline. The park typically has play areas and open grass for children, picnic spots, and space to relax with the sea breeze, making it popular with local families.

item.title: Hakuto Onsen & the White Rabbit Myth Coast — Guide
item.description: Hakuto Onsen sits on the Sea of Japan coast west of Tottori city, in an area steeped in one of Japan’s oldest myths: the tale of the White Rabbit of Inaba, recorded in the eighth-century Kojiki. In the story a rabbit, skinned by crocodiles, is healed by the kind deity Okuninushi, who then wins the hand of a princess — making the site a place associated with healing and, because of the romance, with en-musubi, the matchmaking of good relationships.

item.title: Himuka / Hyuga Coast Scenic Drive — Guide
item.description: Miyazaki’s coastline offers superb scenic driving not only south along the Nichinan Coast but also north around the Hyuga area, where the dramatic ‘Himuka’ coast features some of the prefecture’s most striking sea scenery. The star attraction is Cape Umagase (Umagase), where sheer cliffs of columnar volcanic rock — formed by ancient lava flows and eroded into remarkable regular pillars — drop dramatically into the deep blue sea, viewed from clifftop walkways and lookouts.

item.title: Itoshima Peninsula and Futamigaura Beach — Guide
item.description: The Itoshima Peninsula, a short drive west of Fukuoka city, has become one of the region’s most popular getaways — a relaxed stretch of coastline mixing beaches, surf, farm produce and a thriving scene of stylish seaside cafes, bakeries and craft studios. Its most photogenic sight is Futamigaura, where a pair of sacred ‘married rocks’ (meoto-iwa) linked by a sacred rope stand in the sea beside a striking white torii gate, framing spectacular sunsets over the water.

item.title: Karatsu Castle: The Castle by the Sea — Guide
item.description: Karatsu Castle stands on a low hill above the sea where the Matsuura River flows into Karatsu Bay, its white walls and tiled roofs looking especially graceful against the water — earning it the nickname ‘Maizuru-jo’ (dancing crane castle) and, for the way it seems to float above the coast, the ‘floating castle’. Though the present keep is a modern reconstruction, its hilltop setting is superb: from the top there are sweeping views over the bay, the town, and the famous Niji-no-Matsubara, a two-hundred-year-old pine grove stretching several kilometres along the shore.

item.title: Motonosumi Shrine: 123 Torii Above the Sea — Guide
item.description: Motonosumi Shrine occupies one of the most spectacular settings in western Japan: a green headland on the rugged Nagato coast where 123 vivid vermilion torii gates march in a winding line down the slope toward cliffs and the deep blue Sea of Japan below. Founded in the twentieth century and dedicated to prosperity and good fortune, it was named by an American broadcaster as one of Japan’s most beautiful places, and the sight of the red gates against green grass, white surf and blue sea is unforgettable.

item.title: Nagato Citrus: Mikan Picking on the Coast — Guide
item.description: The warm, sunlit coast around Nagato in northern Yamaguchi is ideal citrus country, and the area is known for its mikan — the small, sweet, easy-peel mandarin oranges that are a staple of Japanese autumn and winter. In season, orchards on the hillsides open for fruit picking, letting visitors wander among the trees, pick sun-ripened mikan straight from the branch, and eat their fill of the sweet, juicy fruit. Set against the backdrop of the scenic Nagato coast and the islands offshore, it is a relaxed, family-friendly outing and a refreshing, healthy taste of the region — a gentle counterpoint to Nagato’s dramatic shrine and wilder coastline.

item.title: Sakurajima & Osumi Cycling — Guide
item.description: Cycling is a wonderful way to experience the dramatic scenery around Sakurajima and the Osumi Peninsula in Kagoshima. Sakurajima island itself has a roughly 36 km road looping most of the way around it, and cycling here takes you past solidified lava fields, seaside footbaths, observation points with close-up volcano views, small villages and fertile fields of volcanic-soil produce, with the smoking cone as a constant backdrop. Rental bikes, including e-bikes to help with the hills, are available near the ferry terminal.

item.title: Shingu Beach and the Genkai Coast — Guide
item.description: North of Fukuoka city, the town of Shingu sits on the coast within the Genkai Quasi-National Park, a protected stretch of the scenic Genkai Sea coastline known for clean beaches, pine groves and offshore islands. Shingu’s beach is a pleasant, relatively uncrowded spot for a seaside stroll or a summer swim, backed by pines and looking out over the sea. From Shingu’s port, a short ferry runs to Ainoshima, a tiny fishing island famous as a ‘cat island’, where a large population of friendly cats roams the sleepy harbour and lanes — a quirky, popular half-day trip for animal lovers.

item.title: The Bungo Strait Coast — Guide
item.description: The Bungo Strait (Bungo Suido) is the stretch of sea separating eastern Kyushu from the island of Shikoku, and Oita’s long coastline along it offers scenic beauty and superb seafood. The strait’s strong tidal currents, where the waters of the Seto Inland Sea meet the Pacific, create rich, oxygenated fishing grounds that produce some of Japan’s most prized fish — above all the famous ‘Seki-saba’ (mackerel) and ‘Seki-aji’ (horse mackerel) caught off Saganoseki, so firm and flavourful they command premium prices nationwide.

item.title: The Nichinan Coast — Guide
item.description: The Nichinan Coast (Nichinan Kaigan) is a beautiful stretch of subtropical coastline running south from Miyazaki city, and one of the most scenic drives in Kyushu. Following the shore along Route 220, the road winds past a succession of dramatic capes, blue Pacific bays, rocky islets, phoenix palm-lined avenues and lush green hills, with viewpoints and rest stops along the way. It links some of Miyazaki’s most famous sights, including the cave shrine of Udo Jingū set in the seaside cliffs, and further south, Cape Toi with its herds of wild horses grazing on the headland.

item.title: The Uwa Sea Coast and Sightseeing Boats — Guide
item.description: The Uwa Sea washes the deeply indented southern coast of Ehime, a beautiful ria coastline of countless inlets, bays and small islands around Uwajima and the Nanyo region. Sheltered and rich in marine life, its calm waters are dotted with the rafts of pearl and fish farms — this is a major area for pearl cultivation and aquaculture — and backed by steep, citrus-clad hills. Sightseeing boats explore the scenery, weaving among the islands and past the coastal fishing villages, while the coast itself offers scenic drives, viewpoints and quiet beaches.

item.title: Tottori Seashore Park: Green Space by the Sea — Guide
item.description: Tottori’s seashore park is a broad, well-kept coastal green space near the sand dunes, offering a gentle counterpoint to the stark desert landscape just along the coast. Wide lawns, seasonal flower beds, tree-lined paths and open views over the Sea of Japan make it a relaxed spot for a walk, a picnic or letting children run around, popular with local families at weekends. Depending on the season it colours with flowers, and its paths and viewpoints look out over the same coastline that produces the famous dunes — a calm, uncrowded green break rather than a headline attraction.

item.title: Ushimado: The 'Aegean of Japan' Coast — Guide
item.description: Ushimado, on the Inland Sea coast east of Okayama city, has long been marketed as the ‘Aegean of Japan’, a nickname earned by its unusually sunny, dry climate, whitewashed buildings and the scatter of small green islands offshore. The centrepiece is the Ushimado Olive Garden, a hillside grove of some two thousand olive trees with a cafe and a viewing terrace looking out over the strait. Below, the old port keeps traces of its history as a stop for Korean diplomatic missions to Edo, and yacht harbours and quiet beaches line the shore.

item.title: Kujukuri Beach Guide: Japan's Longest Beach & Access
item.description: Stretching some 60 kilometres in a near-straight line down Chiba’s Pacific coast, Kujukuri Beach is one of the longest beaches in Japan — an immense ribbon of sand, surf and big sky. Its name (“99 ri”) nods to its legendary length, and its open eastern aspect makes it a famous spot to watch the sunrise over the ocean. Long a centre of the iwashi (sardine) fishing industry, today it’s a summer playground for swimming, surfing, beachcombing and seaside seafood, with a refreshingly wild, uncommercialised feel.

item.title: Miura Peninsula Guide: Beaches, Capes & Access
item.description: Jutting into the sea south of Yokohama, the Miura Peninsula is Kanagawa’s breezy coastal escape — a rural finger of land ringed by beaches, fishing ports, sea cliffs and flower fields, all within easy reach of Tokyo. At its tip sits Misaki, a famous tuna port, and the rugged little island of Jogashima with its lighthouse and walking trails. In between are swimming beaches, the science-museum coast of Aburatsubo, seasonal blooms and farm stands piled with Miura’s prized vegetables.

item.title: Onjuku & Southern Boso Coast Guide: Beaches & Access
item.description: The breezy resort town of Onjuku, on Chiba’s outer Boso coast, is a classic Japanese seaside escape — a crescent of white sand and turquoise shallows that has drawn beachgoers since the early 20th century. Gentle, clean and family-friendly, Onjuku Beach is great for swimming and lazing, watched over by a quirky “Tsukimi” mermaid statue and a monument commemorating the 1609 rescue of shipwrecked Spanish sailors bound for Mexico (the town’s enduring link to Acapulco).

item.title: Shakotan Peninsula Guide: Cape Kamui, Blue Sea & Uni
item.description: West of Otaru, the rugged Shakotan Peninsula is famous for one thing above all: the colour of its sea. The vivid, jewel-like “Shakotan Blue” glows beneath dramatic cliffs and capes, making this one of Hokkaido’s most beautiful stretches of coast and its only marine park. Walk out to wild Cape Kamui and Cape Shimamui for sweeping ocean views, then feast on the region’s celebrated summer sea urchin (uni), served gloriously fresh on rice.

item.title: Shonan Coast Guide: Beaches, Enoden & Access
item.description: The Shonan coast is the Tokyo area’s beloved beach playground — a sunny, laid-back stretch of sand and surf running from Kamakura past Enoshima toward Hiratsuka, all under the gaze of Mt. Fuji on clear days. This is where city-dwellers come to swim, surf, cycle and watch the sunset, riding the charming retro Enoden train as it rattles between the sea and old neighbourhoods. With beaches, Enoshima island, fresh shirasu, and an easygoing California-meets-Japan vibe, Shonan is the perfect seaside complement to historic Kamakura.

item.title: Iwate Nature: Sanriku Coast, Iwate-san Volcano & Hayachine Mountain
item.description: Iwate Prefecture Nature & Outdoor Guide for International Visitors Stretching from the Pacific coast to mountainous interior highlands, Iwate Prefecture offers some of northern Japan’s most spectacular and unspoiled natural landscapes. This guide covers essential outdoor destinations, from dramatic coastal cliffs to sacred peaks and ancient limestone caves. 1. Sanriku Fukko National Park: Where Mountains Meet the Sea The Landscape The Sanriku coast is Japan’s premier example of ria coastline—a drowned river valley landscape where ancient mountains have been partially submerged, creating a complex shoreline of deep inlets, rugged headlands, and isolated coves.

item.title: Hyogo Nature: Mt. Rokko, Awaji Island & Coastal Trails
item.description: Hyogo Prefecture stretches across one of Japan’s most geographically diverse corridors, running from the Pacific-facing shores of the Seto Inland Sea all the way north to the dramatic cliffs and hidden beaches of the Sea of Japan coast. Between these two edges lies an interior of forested mountains, river valleys, and historic castle towns. Few Japanese prefectures can offer a visitor alpine wildflower meadows, oceanic tidal whirlpools, fishing village seascapes, and terraced rural farmland within a single day’s travel.

item.title: Tottori Nature Guide: Uradome Coast, Mount Daisen & Seasonal Landscapes
item.description: Tottori’s natural variety is compressed into a narrow geography: a coastline of dunes, sea cliffs, and beaches, then an immediate rise to 1,700m mountain peaks. The San’in coast is one of Japan’s most geologically active stretches of shoreline; the inland mountains carry some of the country’s finest beech forest. The prefecture’s low population density means these landscapes see a fraction of the visitors that equivalent sites in Kyushu or Chubu would attract.

item.title: Kanagawa Nature Guide: Hakone Volcanoes, Kamakura Trails & Shonan Coast
item.description: Kanagawa contains more ecological variety than any other prefecture near Tokyo. Within 90 minutes of Shinjuku you can stand inside an active volcanic crater, hike a mountain ridge used by samurai armies, surf a Pacific beach, or kayak among sea caves on a wild volcanic cape. The prefecture is almost entirely overlooked by nature travellers who default to the Japanese Alps — a significant mistake. item.title: San-in Coast Japan Guide 2026: Shimane & Tottori
item.description: San-in Coast Japan: The Ultimate Travel Guide to Shimane & Tottori (2024–2025) Discover Japan’s most overlooked coastline — where ancient myths, towering sand dunes, and soul-warming seafood await far from the tourist crowds. If you’ve been to Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka and felt the crush of overtourism, the San-in coast of Japan is the antidote you didn’t know you needed. Stretching along the Sea of Japan across Shimane and Tottori prefectures, this region — collectively known as San-in — offers a travel experience that feels like stepping into an older, quieter, more generous Japan.

item.title: San-in Coast Japan Hidden Travel Route Guide 2026
item.description: San-in Coast Japan Hidden Travel Route: The Ultimate Guide to Japan’s Most Underrated Coastline If you’ve already visited Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka, and you’re craving something entirely different — somewhere the tour buses don’t go, where the landscapes feel untouched, and where a fisherman might invite you to try his morning catch — then the San-in coast Japan hidden travel route is exactly what you’re looking for. Stretching along the Sea of Japan side of western Honshu through Tottori and Shimane prefectures, this is the Japan that most foreign visitors never see.
